# Settings reference

Every setting app-tail stores, written out from the same registry the agent, the CLI
and the dashboard read. If a setting exists, it is on this page, with the default it
starts at and when a change to it takes effect.

Most people never need this page: the dashboard shows the everyday settings on each
feature's own card and keeps the rest behind **Advanced settings**. It is here for scripting,
fleet setups and anyone who wants to see every knob at once.

## Changing a setting

| From | How |
|---|---|
| Dashboard | **Settings** in the side rail, or the settings on each feature's card. |
| CLI, one setting | `app-tail settings set <key> <value>`, where the key is either name in the first two columns. |
| CLI, several at once | `app-tail settings set --udp-timeout=120 --show-tray=true` |
| Terminal menu | `app-tail settings menu` |
| Read one back | `app-tail settings get <key>`, or `app-tail settings list` for all of them. |
| API | `PUT /api/settings` with a JSON body keyed by the setting's key. Every API call carries the token; see [the API reference](api.md#authentication). |

Lists are comma separated on the command line and JSON arrays over the API. Secrets are
write-only everywhere: the agent reports whether one is stored, never what it is.

**Takes effect** says what a change needs before it is fully in force:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| at once | The running agent picks it up immediately. |
| at once, while connected | Pushed to the running Tailscale connection. A change made while it is down is kept and applied when it next comes up. |
| after `app-tail restart` | Rebuilds the Tailscale connection inside the running agent. The dashboard and the CLI say when one is due. |
| after app-tail restarts | The whole program has to stop and start again. |
| next start | Read once when app-tail starts. |

Settings marked *Advanced* sit behind **Advanced settings** in the dashboard. A
setting that belongs to a feature only does anything while that feature's switch is on;
its description names the switch.

## Feature switches

Each optional feature has one switch that turns the whole of it on or off.

| Feature | Switch | CLI | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advanced networking | `advancedNetworking` | `--advanced-networking` | Settings for joining a coordination server other than Tailscale's, such as a self-hosted Headscale. |
| Tailnet proxy | `proxy.enabled` | `--proxy` | Run a loopback SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy so any program on this machine can reach tailnet devices by IP and MagicDNS name, without a VPN interface. |
| Automatic ports | `automap.enabled` | `--automap` | Open a fixed local port for every device on the tailnet, so peer.local:22 becomes localhost:14002 and stays there across restarts. |
| Exit node | `exitNode.enabled` | `--exit-node` | Route this device's other traffic through a device on your tailnet. app-tail routes in userspace, so this applies to what goes through its proxy and its forwards rather than to every program on this machine. |
| Subnet routes | `routes.enabled` | `--routes` | Reach the private networks other devices advertise. app-tail routes in userspace, so those networks are reachable through its proxy and its forwards rather than from every program on this machine. |
| Tailnet DNS | `dns.enabled` | `--dns` | Resolve names with your tailnet's own DNS, including split-DNS domains pointed at a private nameserver. This applies to what app-tail looks up; it changes nothing about how other programs on this machine resolve names. |
| System resolver | `systemDns.enabled` | `--system-dns` | Choose which DNS servers this whole machine uses, including DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS, and switch between them in one click. Names that belong to the network you are on keep resolving through that network. This is one of the two modules that change the machine rather than only app-tail: it needs administrator rights once, and it puts your settings back when it is switched off. |
| Blocking | `dnsBlock.enabled` | `--dns-block` | Refuse names on lists you choose -- Hagezi, StevenBlack, OISD, threat feeds -- rather than resolving them. The lists are downloaded and matched on this machine, and two separate switches say where they apply: to what app-tail itself looks up, and to what the whole machine looks up. |
| Security | `security.enabled` | `--security` | Block incoming tailnet connections, and choose whether this device reports posture information about itself back to your tailnet. |
| Network interface | `interface.enabled` | `--interface` | Create a real network interface so tailnet addresses and MagicDNS names work in every program on this machine, with nothing to configure per program. This is the only module that changes the machine: it needs a privileged helper, and it writes routes and resolver files outside app-tail's own directory. |
| Logs | `telemetry.enabled` | `--telemetry` | Keep a history of what this app did: the tailnet node connecting and dropping, forwards starting and stopping, the resolver being claimed and put back, and every settings change. It records nothing until you turn it on, keeps what it records in memory only unless you also turn on storing it, and sends none of it anywhere. |
| Traffic inspection | `ips.enabled` | `--ips` | Examine every connection app-tail carries against lists of names and addresses, and report the ones that match. It starts by reporting only: nothing is refused until you say so, so you can see what it would have stopped before it stops anything. It reads what app-tail carries and nothing else, and matches it on this machine. |

| `hostnameTemplate` | `--hostname-template` | text | `app-tail-{hostname}` | after `app-tail restart` | **Hostname template**<br>Template used when no explicit hostname is set (tokens: {hostname}, {id}). Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Overridden by `APPTAIL_HOSTNAME_TEMPLATE` when set. *Advanced.* |
| `tags` | `--tags` | list | `tag:app-tail` | after `app-tail restart` | **Tags**<br>Tailnet tags to advertise, comma separated. Required when enrolling with an OAuth client secret, and the tags must already exist in the tailnet. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Overridden by `APPTAIL_TAGS` when set. *Advanced.* |
| `advertiseTagsOnLogin` | `--advertise-tags-on-login` | on/off | off | after `app-tail restart` | **Advertise tags on browser login**<br>Advertise the tags during an interactive browser login. The signed-in user must own them in tagOwners or the login is refused. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Overridden by `APPTAIL_ADVERTISE_TAGS_ON_LOGIN` when set. *Advanced.* |
| `effectiveHostname` |  | text |  | at once | **Effective device name**<br>The name this connection actually presents after the template renders (read-only). Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Read-only, worked out from other settings. |

## Tailnet

Which coordination server this device joins, and how it registers.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `advancedNetworking` | `--advanced-networking` | on/off | off | after `app-tail restart` | **Advanced networking**<br>Reveal the settings for joining a coordination server other than Tailscale's. Turning it back off returns them to their defaults. Turns the whole Advanced networking feature on or off. |
| `controlURL` | `--control-url` | URL | not set | after `app-tail restart` | **Control server URL**<br>Coordination server URL. Leave empty unless you run Headscale or similar. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `advancedNetworking` is on. Overridden by `APPTAIL_CONTROL_URL` when set. *Advanced.* |
| `ephemeral` | `--ephemeral` | on/off | off | after `app-tail restart` | **Ephemeral node**<br>Remove this device from the tailnet when the agent exits. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Overridden by `APPTAIL_EPHEMERAL` when set. *Advanced.* |
| `tailnet.repairRoutes` | `--repair-tailnet-routes` | on/off | on | at once | **Put the tailnet's route back when it goes missing**<br>Watch for this machine losing the route to the tailnet's address range while still carrying the tailnet's addresses, and put that route back on the interface already holding them. It is the one fault a tailnet client cannot report: the client stays connected and its own probes to every device keep answering, while every ordinary program on this machine sends tailnet traffic out of the physical network instead and times out. Nothing else is touched -- the range is the tailnet's own and the interface has to be one already carrying it. *Advanced.* |

| `udpBufferBytes` | `--udp-buffer` | number, 0 to 65535 | 65535 | at once | **UDP buffer (bytes)**<br>Largest UDP datagram a forward can relay. 65535 is the protocol maximum. *Advanced.* |

## Proxy

A loopback proxy that reaches the whole tailnet, for programs you point at it.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `proxy.enabled` | `--proxy` | on/off | off | at once | **Tailnet proxy**<br>Run a loopback SOCKS5 and HTTP proxy that reaches the whole tailnet. While it is on, any program running as any user on this machine can reach every device your ACLs allow this node to reach. Turns the whole Tailnet proxy feature on or off. |
| `proxy.listenAddr` | `--proxy-addr` | address:port | `127.0.0.1:1080` | at once | **Proxy address**<br>Loopback host:port this instance listens on. A loopback bind is the only thing keeping it off the network, since a proxy has no credential by default. Two instances cannot ask for the same port. Moved to the proxy "default"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. |
| `proxy.scope` | `--proxy-scope` | one of `tailnet`, `all`, `custom` |  | at once | **What this proxy will reach**<br>A reading of the rules below: whether they carry one connection, also carry what this machine reaches on its own, or say something the two old settings could not. Moved to the proxy "default"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. Read-only, worked out from other settings. Deprecated: how far a proxy dials is now the rules below, which can grant one port on one connection instead of a whole network; this reads back what they amount to |
| `proxy.resolveVia` | `--proxy-resolve-via` | one of `netmap`, `tailnet` | `netmap` | at once | **Resolve names with**<br>Which resolver turns a name into an address. Only the tailnet's own knows about a split-DNS domain, so a name that resolves everywhere except through the proxy is what this setting is for. Moved to the proxy "default"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `proxy.requireToken` | `--proxy-require-token` | on/off | off | at once | **Require a password**<br>Make this instance demand the password below. A PAC file has nowhere to put a password, so turning this on stops browsers configured by PAC from using it. Moved to the proxy "default"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `proxy.token` | `--proxy-token` | secret | write-only | at once | **Proxy password**<br>The password this instance demands, with the username app-tail. Write-only: a stored password is never sent back out. Moved to the proxy "default"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `proxy.dialTimeoutSec` | `--proxy-dial-timeout` | number, 0 to 600 | 30 | at once | **Dial timeout (s)**<br>How long one connection through this instance may take to establish. A first connection to a sleeping device negotiates a path first, so this is longer than a local dial would need. Zero uses the default. Moved to the proxy "default"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `proxy.system` | `--proxy-system` | on/off | off | at once | **Point this machine's proxy settings at it**<br>Write the auto-config URL into this Windows account's own proxy settings, so programs that read them need no setup. It is put back as it was when this is turned off. Firefox and most command-line tools keep their own setting. Does something only while `proxy.enabled` is on. |

## Automatic ports

Give every device on the tailnet a fixed local port, so a peer's SSH or web port is reachable at localhost without configuring anything per device.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `automap.enabled` | `--automap` | on/off | off | at once | **Open a port for every device**<br>Open a local port for every device on the tailnet, so a peer's SSH or web port is reachable at localhost. Each port is assigned once and kept, so anything you save that names it keeps working. Turns the whole Automatic ports feature on or off. |
| `automap.ports` | `--automap-ports` | list | `22` | at once | **Ports to map**<br>Which port on each device to map. Every device gets one local port per entry, so a long list multiplied by a large tailnet reaches the limit fast. Does something only while `automap.enabled` is on. |
| `automap.max` | `--automap-max` | number, 0 to 512 | 32 | at once | **Most ports to open**<br>How many local ports the module will open at once. Devices are taken online-first, then by name; anything past the limit is reported rather than quietly left out. Zero uses the default. Does something only while `automap.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `automap.portBase` | `--automap-port-base` | number, 0 to 65535 | 14000 | at once | **First port to use**<br>Where the search for a free local port starts. Changing it does not move ports already assigned; those are kept so nothing that names one breaks. Zero uses the default. Does something only while `automap.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

| `exitNode.nodeId` | `--exit-node-id` | tailnet device | not set | at once, while connected | **Device to route through**<br>The device your traffic leaves from, chosen from the ones your tailnet offers as exit nodes. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. |
| `exitNode.auto` | `--exit-node-auto` | on/off | off | at once, while connected | **Let Tailscale choose**<br>Let the tailnet pick the exit node and keep re-picking it. Only devices your network marks as suggestable are considered, which on most tailnets means Tailscale's own Mullvad nodes rather than one you run yourself. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. |
| `exitNode.allowLanAccess` | `--exit-node-allow-lan` | on/off | off | at once, while connected | **Keep reaching this machine's own network**<br>Keep the printers, NAS and routers on the network this machine is plugged into reachable while the exit node carries everything else. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. |
| `exitNode.onFailure` | `--exit-node-on-failure` | one of `hold`, `next`, `off` | `hold` | at once | **When it goes offline**<br>What to do when the exit node in use stops being reachable. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `exitNode.rotate.enabled` | `--exit-node-rotate` | on/off | off | at once | **Move between exit nodes**<br>Change exit node on a schedule, so no single one sees all of this device's traffic. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `exitNode.rotate.strategy` | `--exit-node-rotate-strategy` | one of `round_robin`, `random`, `latency` | `round_robin` | at once | **How to choose the next one**<br>Which exit node the schedule moves to next. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `exitNode.rotate.intervalSec` | `--exit-node-rotate-interval` | number, 0 to 86400 | 900 | at once | **How long to stay on one (s)**<br>How long one exit node is used before the next is chosen. The lower limit is a minute because every switch drops the connections through the old device, and rotating faster than that is an outage this device inflicts on itself. Zero uses the default. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `exitNode.rotate.pauseOnActive` | `--exit-node-rotate-pause` | on/off | on | at once | **Wait for connections to finish**<br>Hold a scheduled switch back while connections are still open through the current exit node, so a download in progress is not cut off. The hold is bounded by the setting below. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `exitNode.rotate.maxDeferrals` | `--exit-node-rotate-max-deferrals` | number, 0 to 100 | 3 | at once | **Turns to skip while busy**<br>How many scheduled switches may be skipped while connections stay open before one happens anyway. Without a limit a machine that is never idle would keep one exit node forever, which is the opposite of rotating. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `exitNode.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

## DNS

Which resolver app-tail uses for the names it looks up. It configures nothing outside this app: every other program on this machine keeps resolving as it does now.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dns.enabled` | `--dns` | on/off | off | at once | **Use tailnet DNS**<br>Turn on the setting that decides which resolver app-tail uses for the names it looks up. Nothing changes until you choose below. Turns the whole Tailnet DNS feature on or off. |
| `dns.useTailnet` | `--dns-use-tailnet` | on/off | off | at once, while connected | **Resolve names with your tailnet's DNS**<br>Point app-tail's own resolver at the nameservers your tailnet publishes, including split-DNS domains aimed at a private nameserver. This applies to names app-tail looks up -- through its proxy and its forwards -- and to nothing else: no resolv.conf, no scutil entry and no NRPT rule is written, so every other program on this machine resolves exactly as it does now. Changing what the rest of the machine resolves with is the System resolver module, which is a separate switch. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `dns.enabled` is on. |
| `dns.zone` | `--dns-zone` | text | `internal` | at once | **Name every connection under**<br>The parent of every connection's own names: with this at its default, a host called db on the connection whose short name is office is db.office.internal. It is what lets two networks that use the same addresses both be reached at once, since the name says which one you meant and the address cannot. Changing it renames every connection's suffix, so anything that already names one has to be updated. *Advanced.* |

## System resolver

Which resolver this whole machine uses. This and the network interface are the two parts of app-tail that change the machine rather than only itself: while it is on, every program here resolves names through app-tail, and it is put back when app-tail stops.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `systemDns.enabled` | `--system-dns` | on/off | off | at once | **Use a chosen resolver for this machine**<br>Point every program on this machine at the resolver you choose below. This is one of the two things app-tail changes outside itself: it needs administrator rights once, it lists exactly what it changes, and it puts your previous settings back when you turn it off. Nothing changes while the profile below is System default. Turns the whole System resolver feature on or off. |
| `systemDns.profile` | `--system-dns-profile` | DNS profile | `system` | at once | **Resolver**<br>Which set of DNS servers this machine resolves names through. System default leaves the machine exactly as it is. Switching is immediate, which is the point: a resolver that blocks a site you need is one click away from one that does not. Does something only while `systemDns.enabled` is on. |
| `systemDns.bootstrapProfile` | `--system-dns-bootstrap` | DNS profile | `quad9` | at once | **Look resolver hostnames up through**<br>A resolver written as a hostname -- tls://dns.nextdns.io, an https:// URL -- has to be turned into an address before app-tail can reach it, and that one lookup cannot go to the resolver being looked up. It goes here instead. Keep it on an encrypted profile: that lookup is the one part of the chain this network can still answer, and an answer of its choosing makes your resolver unreachable rather than wrong, since the certificate is checked against the hostname either way. System default sends it to this network's resolvers, which is also what happens if the profile here cannot be reached. Does something only while `systemDns.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `systemDns.localSuffixes` | `--system-dns-local-suffixes` | list | none | at once | **Names this network answers for**<br>Extra name suffixes to look up through the network you are on rather than through the resolver above. app-tail already sends single names, .local, anything under a private address range and the names this network publishes that way; this is for a suffix it cannot know about. Does something only while `systemDns.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `systemDns.retryOnNxdomain` | `--system-dns-retry-nxdomain` | on/off | off | at once | **Ask this network again for a name the resolver says does not exist**<br>Off, and worth leaving off. A resolver that filters a domain -- NextDNS, Pi-hole, a family filter -- blocks it by answering that it does not exist, so asking a second resolver afterwards is how a blocklist stops blocking. Turn it on only if names on this network are genuinely coming back missing. Does something only while `systemDns.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `systemDns.listenAddr` | `--system-dns-addr` | address:port | `127.0.0.153:53` | at once | **Where app-tail answers DNS**<br>Loopback host:port app-tail's own resolver listens on, and what this machine is pointed at. Nothing outside this machine can reach it. Change it only if something here already holds the default; app-tail moves to another loopback address by itself if it cannot take this one. Does something only while `systemDns.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

## Blocking

Refuse names that appear on lists you choose -- advertising, tracking, malware -- instead of resolving them. The lists are downloaded, kept on this machine and matched here, so nothing about which names you look up leaves this device.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dnsBlock.enabled` | `--dns-block` | on/off | off | at once | **Block names on a list**<br>Download the lists you choose and refuse the names on them instead of looking them up. Turning this on starts the downloads; the two switches below say where the lists apply, and until one of them is on nothing is blocked anywhere. Turns the whole Blocking feature on or off. |
| `dnsBlock.own` | `--dns-block-own` | on/off | off | at once | **Block what app-tail looks up**<br>Refuse a blocked name when app-tail resolves it: what its proxy dials, and what an automatic port reaches. A port forward is unaffected -- it hands the target you configured straight to the other end without ever looking a name up here. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. |
| `dnsBlock.system` | `--dns-block-system` | on/off | on | at once | **Block what this machine looks up**<br>Refuse a blocked name for every program on this machine, which is what an ad blocker for the whole device means. It does nothing on its own: the machine only asks app-tail at all while the system resolver in the section above is on. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. |
| `dnsBlock.answer` | `--dns-block-answer` | one of `nxdomain`, `sinkhole`, `refused` | `nxdomain` | at once | **Answer a blocked name with**<br>What a program is told when it asks for a blocked name. All three stop the connection; they differ in what the program does next. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `dnsBlock.lists` | `--dns-block-lists` | list | `hagezi-pro` | at once | **Lists in use**<br>The ids of the lists that are switched on, which the switches on the card above write for you. Every list here is downloaded and matched; a list you have added but not switched on is kept and costs nothing. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `dnsBlock.refreshHours` | `--dns-block-refresh-hours` | number, 0 to 720 | 1 | at once | **Re-download a list after**<br>Hours before a list is fetched again. The lists themselves are rebuilt about once a day. A copy that cannot be fetched keeps blocking from disk rather than expiring, so a long interval costs coverage, never blocking itself. Zero uses the default. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `dnsBlock.allow` | `--dns-block-allow` | list | none | at once | **Never block**<br>Names that resolve normally whatever any list says, each covering everything under it. This is what a wrongly blocked site is fixed with, so it beats every list and the one you added yourself. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. |
| `dnsBlock.deny` | `--dns-block-deny` | list | none | at once | **Always block**<br>Names blocked with no list involved, each covering everything under it. The list above wins where the two disagree. Does something only while `dnsBlock.enabled` is on. |

## Traffic inspection

Examine the connections app-tail carries and report the ones that match the domains and addresses you name, or refuse them outright. It sees what app-tail itself carries -- the network interface in fabric mode, the proxy, and connections other devices route through this one -- and nothing this machine sends any other way.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ips.enabled` | `--ips` | on/off | off | at once | **Inspect the traffic app-tail carries**<br>Compare every connection app-tail carries against the entries below and record the ones that match. Turning this on starts the matching; the two switches below say what is examined, and until one of them is on nothing is examined anywhere. Turns the whole Traffic inspection feature on or off. |
| `ips.mode` | `--ips-mode` | one of `detect`, `prevent` | `detect` | at once | **When a connection matches**<br>What happens to a connection that matches an entry. Both record the match; they differ in whether the connection is still made. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. |
| `ips.names` | `--ips-names` | on/off | on | at once | **Examine the names asked for**<br>Match the name a program asked for, before it is looked up. This is what app-tail's own resolver and its proxy see; a program that dials an address directly never gave a name here, and is reached by the switch below instead. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. |
| `ips.destinations` | `--ips-destinations` | on/off | on | at once | **Examine where connections are bound**<br>Match the address a connection is bound for. This is all the network interface and the subnet router ever have, and it is the half that still applies when a program brings its own resolver or dials an address it hardcoded. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. |
| `ips.anomaly` | `--ips-anomaly` | on/off | off | at once | **Watch for unusual patterns**<br>Report what a run of connections adds up to, rather than what any one of them is bound for: one device reaching many ports on another, one reaching a great many addresses at once, and data leaving inside DNS queries. This matches against no list, so it works on a machine where nothing has been typed above. It is the only part of inspection that keeps a record of where traffic went; that record is held in memory for a minute, is never written to disk, and is discarded when you turn this off. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.handshake` | `--ips-handshake` | on/off | off | at once | **Read the start of each connection**<br>Read the first few kilobytes a connection sends, where the name it is really for lives: the server name inside a TLS handshake and the host of a plain web request. This is what reaches a program that never asked app-tail for a name and dialled an address instead. Nothing after the opening is read, and nothing is decrypted: the name is sent in the clear before the encryption starts. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.fingerprints` | `--ips-fingerprints` | on/off | off | at once | **Note which software opened the connection**<br>Record a short fingerprint of how each TLS connection was opened, which says which family of software made it. It is a note on a finding rather than something matched against: everything built on the same library shares one, and anyone who wants theirs changed can change it. Needs the setting above. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.payload` | `--ips-payload` | on/off | off | at once | **Look for your own byte patterns**<br>Read the same opening bytes against the patterns below, which is the one part of inspection that looks at what a connection carries rather than where it is going. Nothing is decrypted, so this reaches only what is sent in the clear. It also holds those few kilobytes for the whole opening of each connection instead of letting them go as soon as the connection is named. Needs the setting above. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.signatures` | `--ips-signatures` | list | none | at once | **Byte patterns to look for**<br>One pattern per entry, written as a name, an equals sign, and the bytes in quotes. Use \xNN inside the quotes for a byte that is not text. The name is what a finding is reported as; the bytes are never written to a log or shown on a card, so a pattern can safely be something you are watching for a leak of. Matching is exact, including case, and a pattern must be at least four bytes: anything shorter appears in nearly every connection. There is no feed for these and no built-in set -- no maintained list of stream patterns exists to download, so these are yours. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.lists` | `--ips-lists` | list | none | at once | **Feeds in use**<br>The ids of the address feeds that are switched on, which the switches on the card above write for you. Every feed here is downloaded and matched; a feed you have added but not switched on is kept and costs nothing. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.refreshHours` | `--ips-refresh-hours` | number, 0 to 720 | 24 | at once | **Re-download a feed after**<br>Hours before a feed is fetched again. These feeds are rebuilt about once a day. A copy that cannot be fetched keeps matching from disk rather than expiring, so a long interval costs coverage, never matching itself. Zero uses the default. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.allow` | `--ips-allow` | list | none | at once | **Never match**<br>Names and networks that are carried whatever any other entry says. A name here covers everything under it. This is what a wrongly refused connection is fixed with, so it beats every entry below, however specific that entry is. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. |
| `ips.deny` | `--ips-deny` | list | none | at once | **Always match**<br>Names, addresses and networks to match on. A name covers everything under it, and an address on its own means that address alone. The list above wins where the two disagree. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. |
| `ips.intercept` | `--ips-intercept` | one of `off`, `only`, `except` | `off` | at once | **Open encrypted connections**<br>Read what encrypted connections carry, rather than only the name they are for. app-tail does this by ending the connection here and starting its own to the real server, presenting a certificate it signed with a root it generated on this machine. Nothing accepts that certificate until you install the root yourself, and nothing happens here at all until you have read what installing it means and said so. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.interceptAgreed` | `--ips-intercept-agreed` | on/off | off | at once | **I have read what opening connections means**<br>Opening connections needs a root certificate installed on this machine. Anything that holds its private key can present a certificate for any site on the internet that this machine will accept, and that stays true until the root is removed from the trust store -- removing app-tail does not remove it. The key is generated here and never leaves the machine. Nothing is opened while this is off, whatever the setting above says. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.interceptOnly` | `--ips-intercept-only` | list | none | at once | **Destinations to open**<br>The destinations opened when the setting above is set to open only what you name. A name covers everything under it, and a network covers every address in it. Nothing else is opened. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `ips.interceptExcept` | `--ips-intercept-except` | list | none | at once | **Destinations to leave alone**<br>The destinations left untouched when the setting above is set to open everything else. Left empty this is the shipped list, which covers software that checks its own certificates and stops working when a connection is opened -- software updates, push notifications, messaging clients. Anything written here replaces that list rather than adding to it, so start from the shipped one and edit it. Does something only while `ips.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

## Security

What this device accepts from the tailnet and what it reports back about itself.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `security.enabled` | `--security` | on/off | off | at once | **Security settings**<br>Turn on the settings that decide what this device accepts from the tailnet and what it reports about itself. Nothing changes until you choose below. Turns the whole Security feature on or off. |
| `security.shieldsUp` | `--shields-up` | on/off | off | at once, while connected | **Refuse incoming tailnet connections**<br>Drop every connection other devices open to this one, whatever your tailnet's ACLs allow. This device can still reach others. Any forward that listens on the tailnet stops answering while this is on, and the forwards table says so. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `security.enabled` is on. |
| `security.postureChecking` | `--posture-checking` | on/off | off | at once, while connected | **Report this device's posture to your tailnet**<br>Send identifying details about this machine -- its serial number, operating system version and any device-management identifiers -- to your tailnet, for admins to write access rules against. That information leaves this machine, so it is off unless you turn it on. Moved to the connection "tailnet"; this key still works and writes there. Does something only while `security.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

## Network interface

Create a real network interface, so the addresses and names on your connections work in every program on this machine -- either the tailnet on its own, or every connection at once. This and the system resolver are the two parts of app-tail that change the machine rather than only itself.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `interface.enabled` | `--interface` | on/off | off | at once | **Offer the network-interface mode**<br>Show the settings for running app-tail on a real network interface. Turning this on changes nothing by itself: the interface is created only once you also choose the mode below. Turns the whole Network interface feature on or off. |
| `interface.mode` | `--interface-mode` | one of `userspace`, `tun`, `fabric` | `userspace` | after `app-tail restart` | **How your networks are reached**<br>Which stack your connections are reached over. Does something only while `interface.enabled` is on. |
| `interface.name` | `--interface-name` | text | not set | after `app-tail restart` | **Interface name**<br>The name to give the interface, or empty for the platform's default. A fixed name is what makes an interface left behind by an unclean exit identifiable, which is what `app-tail tun doctor` reports on. Does something only while `interface.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |
| `interface.virtualPool` | `--interface-virtual-pool` | list of networks (CIDR) | none | after `app-tail restart` | **Ranges to present moved networks from**<br>Where a connection is reached when its own addresses are already taken by another connection or by this machine, comma separated. Leave empty for the range set aside for exactly this (198.18.0.0/15). Only the one-interface-for-every-network mode moves anything: in every other mode nothing is presented anywhere but its own addresses. Does something only while `interface.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

## Live traffic

What this machine is carrying right now: how much is moving, which devices it is moving to, and what has crossed recently.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `traffic.latency` | `--traffic-latency` | on/off | off | at once | **Measure the round trip to each device**<br>Send a small probe to every online device every few seconds and report how long it takes to answer. It is off by default because it is the one part of this page that makes the machine send traffic rather than only report it, which costs battery on a laptop and wakes radios on an idle network. |
| `traffic.smooth` | `--traffic-smooth` | on/off | on | at once | **Smooth the graph lines**<br>Draw the bandwidth graph as a moving average over about the last 25 seconds, weighted toward the middle, so the shape of a transfer is visible through the second-to-second noise. Only that line changes: the rate on the card, the figures per device and the count of open connections are the measured ones either way, and an interval nothing was measured in stays a gap. |

## Logs

Keep a history of what this app did and what it carried, so a fault that has already passed can still be looked at. Nothing is recorded until you turn it on, and everything recorded stays on this machine.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `telemetry.enabled` | `--telemetry` | on/off | off | at once | **Keep a log of what this app does**<br>Record the tailnet node connecting and dropping, forwards starting and stopping, the resolver being claimed and put back, and every settings change, so a fault that has already passed can still be looked at. It is kept in this app's memory, it is never sent anywhere, and it is gone when the app stops. Turns the whole Logs feature on or off. |
| `telemetry.eventLog.retentionDays` | `--telemetry-event-days` | number, 0 to 365 | 30 | at once | **Keep events for**<br>Days an entry stays in the log before it is removed; 0 uses the default of 30. The log also has a fixed size, so a busy machine reaches that limit long before this one. Does something only while `telemetry.enabled` is on. *Advanced.* |

## Application

How the app itself behaves on this machine.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `uiListenAddr` | `--ui-addr` | address:port | `127.0.0.1:0` | after app-tail restarts | **Dashboard address**<br>Loopback host:port the dashboard listens on. Port 0 asks for any free port. When the port is already taken the app runs on one the system assigns for that run and asks for this address again next time. It must stay on loopback: the API token is the only thing between an address reachable off-host and your tailnet identity. Overridden by `APPTAIL_UI_ADDR` when set. *Advanced.* |
| `showTray` | `--show-tray` | on/off | on | next start | **Show tray icon**<br>Show the menu-bar or tray icon. Takes effect on the next start. |
| `autoOpenDashboard` | `--auto-open-dashboard` | on/off | on | at once | **Open the dashboard on first run**<br>Open the dashboard in a browser on first run, when nothing is configured yet. |
| `startAtLogin` | `--start-at-login` | on/off | off | at once | **Start at login**<br>Install a per-user login item so the agent starts when you sign in. No administrator rights needed, except on Windows while a network mode that needs them is selected: there the item is a scheduled task that starts app-tail with those rights, so installing it asks for them once. Changes the operating system's login item rather than the config file. |

Facts about this install.

| `stateDir` |  | text |  | at once | **State directory**<br>Holds the tailnet identity and this configuration. Deleting it forces a new sign-in. Read-only. Overridden by `APPTAIL_STATE_DIR` when set. |
| `machineId` |  | text |  | at once | **Machine ID**<br>Per-install id the {id} hostname token renders to (read-only). Read-only. |

## How app-tail runs here

Which programs on this machine can reach your networks, and how much of the machine app-tail touches to arrange it.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `mode.primary` |  | one of `standalone`, `proxy`, `interface`, `fabric` |  | at once | **Current mode**<br>Read from the switches below rather than set on its own, so choosing a mode and flipping the switches it stands for can never disagree. Read-only, worked out from other settings. |

## Internet traffic

Where everything your connections do not carry goes: out of this machine the way it always has, or through one of your connections so it leaves from there instead.

| Key | CLI flag | Type | Default | Takes effect | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `egress.mode` | `--egress` | one of `direct`, `tunnel`, `multi` | `direct` | at once | **Where internet traffic goes**<br>Traffic to an address none of your connections carries -- the open internet. This does not change what your connections reach; it changes where everything else goes. |
| `egress.tunnelId` | `--egress-connection` | connection | not set | at once | **Connection carrying it**<br>Which connection carries this machine's internet traffic. It is read only while the setting above sends it through a connection: leaving a connection named here while the traffic goes out directly is what lets someone switch back and forth without re-choosing, and it carries nothing until they do. |
| `egress.multi.shape` | `--egress-shape` | one of `spread`, `cascade` | `spread` | at once | **How they carry it**<br>How the connections below carry this machine's internet traffic together. It is read only while the setting above shares the traffic across several connections. |
| `egress.multi.tunnelIds` | `--egress-connections` | list of connections | none | at once | **Connections sharing it**<br>Which connections carry this machine's internet traffic together, in order. Spread between them, the order means nothing and leaving the list empty uses every connection that is running; chained, it is the order the traffic passes through them and the list has to name them. It is read only while the setting above shares the traffic, and while it does, traffic is held rather than sent out of this machine when these connections cannot carry it. |
| `egress.killSwitch` | `--kill-switch` | on/off | off | at once | **Hold it rather than let it out**<br>While the connection above cannot carry this machine's internet traffic, hold the traffic here instead of letting it out over whatever network this machine is on. Nothing falls back: a connection that is down, switched off or not carrying stops the traffic rather than leaking it. It is read only while the setting above sends the traffic through one connection -- several connections already hold it, and sending it out of this machine directly is the setting that says this machine's own network is where it goes. |
